subject: psychology
title: Attachment Theory: Studies and Applications
welcome_lead: Watch the Strange Situation and trace the long shadow of deprivation.
meta_desc: GCSE Psychology adventure on Ainsworth's Strange Situation, attachment types and Bowlby's 44 Thieves.
final_note: You can name attachment types and key supporting studies.

concepts.def: Ainsworth's lab test of attachment in toddlers.
Type B: distressed at separation, soothed easily.
Type A: little distress, avoids caregiver.
Type C: high distress, hard to soothe.
Bowlby's study linking deprivation and crime.

walkthroughs.body_html: Ainsworth observed babies through 8 episodes including caregiver leaving and stranger entering. She classified attachments as secure (B), insecure-avoidant (A) or insecure-resistant (C). Most US infants were secure.

Van Ijzendoorn & Kroonenberg (1988) reviewed 32 studies across 8 countries. Secure attachment was most common everywhere, but Germany had more avoidant infants and Japan/Israel more resistant — culture shapes how attachment shows up.

Bowlby compared 44 young thieves with 44 controls. 14 of the thieves were 'affectionless psychopaths' and 12 of those had suffered prolonged maternal separation. Used to argue deprivation causes later antisocial behaviour, but criticised for retrospective interviews.

options: Always - psychologists can deceive freely.
When demand characteristics would otherwise invalidate the study, with thorough debrief and ethics approval.
Never - deception is always banned.
